messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Roberto is a 65-year-old divorced Latino man who has spent the past eighteen years teaching special education at a public elementary school in San Antonio. He presents for an initial psychological evaluation describing a constellation of symptoms that have quietly eroded his quality of life since his military service decades ago, and which have recently intensified to a degree he can no longer manage alone.

Roberto served as an infantry soldier during a period of sustained combat operations, and the event he identifies as central to his current difficulties occurred during a patrol ambush in which his unit was caught in a narrow corridor under heavy fire. The chaos lasted less than four minutes by his estimate, but within it he experienced a moment of acute disorientation — a wave of dizziness so severe he believed he had been hit — followed by the acrid, metallic taste of blood and smoke that filled his mouth as he pressed himself into the earth. A comrade was shouting his name from somewhere he could not locate. He survived. Several men did not. What lodged itself most deeply was not the sound of the firefight, but the way the dizziness had made him feel utterly unmoored from his own body at the precise moment he needed it most, and the taste that accompanied it — a taste he associates, without entirely being able to explain why, with the moment he understood that death was immediate and indiscriminate.

In the years that followed, Roberto managed. He built a career, raised children, and told himself that what happened overseas was simply the cost of service. But the symptoms never fully receded. They changed shape. Certain experiences began to carry an almost physical charge: the lightheadedness that comes with standing too quickly, the occasional taste of something metallic in cafeteria food, and the specific social pressure of being asked to talk about his service — each of these became capable of pulling him, without warning, back toward the ambush. When these triggers arose, Roberto found that his body moved before his mind could intervene. He began avoiding situations that carried any emotional intensity, steering clear of heated staff meetings, parent conferences that might grow confrontational, or any gathering where he might be asked to speak about himself. He made a habit of positioning himself near doorways — in the faculty lounge, at school assemblies, at his daughter's wedding — so that he could leave without drawing attention. He also began talking about the event as little as possible, deflecting questions from colleagues and family with practiced brevity, because he had learned that even naming what happened was enough to set everything else in motion.

What Roberto could not fully articulate, but what became clear across the first sessions, is that these strategies have not quieted the threat he perceives — they have organised his life around it. He is in a state of near-constant environmental surveillance. In his classroom, he monitors the hallway through the small window in the door, catalogues the positions of the children relative to the exits, and flinches visibly when a locker slams in the corridor outside. Unexpected sounds — a fire drill, a dropped tray in the cafeteria, a car backfiring in the school parking lot — place him on a level of alert that takes the remainder of the day to subside. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels self-evident to him, that he must always know where the exits are before he can allow himself to relax, because relaxation itself feels like exposure. This vigilance, in turn, makes the triggers more potent rather than less: the heightened state of arousal means that a slight dizziness from dehydration or a particular taste in his lunch can register immediately as danger, which sends him back to scanning, checking, positioning himself near the door.

The loop has tightened noticeably in the past year. A new principal introduced a practice of staff sharing personal stories at professional development days. Roberto has begun calling in sick on those mornings. Three colleagues have asked if he is all right. He is not, and he knows it. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last spring when a child in his class vomited and the smell briefly mingled with something that recalled the taste from the ambush — and Roberto found himself at the classroom door, hand on the frame, before he was conscious of having moved. What he most fears is that he is becoming unreliable to children who depend on him. What he most hopes is that he can learn to stay in the room.
